key_findings.finding: The most likely diagnosis is microscopic polyangiitis (MPA), an ANCA-associated small-vessel necrotizing vasculitis. The combination of rapidly progressive renal involvement (hematuria, acute kidney injury, new hypertension), systemic inflammation, skin ischemic ulcers, and gastrointestinal ischemia/bleeding is more consistent with MPA than classic polyarteritis nodosa.

source_tools.relevance: Disease definition identifies MPA as inflammatory necrotizing systemic small-vessel vasculitis.
Review evidence links small-vessel vasculitis to GI ulcer/hemorrhage, skin ulceration, and necrotizing crescentic glomerulonephritis.
Comparison data show glomerulonephritis and ANCA favor MPA/small-vessel disease, whereas classic PAN lacks glomerulonephritis and is more associated with hepatitis B and abnormal angiography.

key_findings.finding: Among the listed laboratory tests, p-ANCA is the most likely positive result, typically reflecting anti-myeloperoxidase (MPO) antibodies. MPA is characteristically associated with p-ANCA/MPO-ANCA; c-ANCA/PR3 is more typical of granulomatosis with polyangiitis.

source_tools.relevance: Search results explicitly state that p-ANCA has high sensitivity/specificity for MPA and that MPA is typically associated with p-ANCA.
Review distinguishes c-ANCA/PR3 from p-ANCA/MPO patterns and associates p-ANCA/MPO with MPA.

key_findings.finding: Classic polyarteritis nodosa remains a differential because of abdominal pain, GI bleeding, skin ischemia, hypertension, and possible hepatitis B association, but PAN generally affects medium arteries, does not cause glomerulonephritis, and is usually ANCA-negative; therefore HBsAg would be expected only if the vignette specifically indicated hepatitis B, not as the best overall answer here.

source_tools.relevance: Comparative study reports hepatitis B antigenemia and hypertension/medium-vessel angiographic abnormalities favor classic PAN, while glomerulonephritis and ANCA favor small-vessel disease/MPA.

key_findings.finding: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis is less likely because the case lacks the characteristic upper-airway granulomatous disease and pulmonary manifestations; c-ANCA/PR3 would be the expected serology if GPA were the diagnosis. Anti-GBM disease is less likely because it does not explain the cutaneous and gastrointestinal vasculitic pattern, while the connective-tissue serologies listed (anti-Ro, anti-Smith, ANA, anti-dsDNA, rheumatoid factor, anticardiolipin) are not the characteristic test for this presentation.

source_tools.relevance: Search results distinguish p-ANCA/MPO orientation toward MPA from c-ANCA/PR3 patterns and describe systemic small-vessel manifestations.
Review summarizes the multisystem vasculitic pattern involving skin, kidneys, and GI tract.
